title: Garden Plot Planner
tagline: Measure · Space it out · Grow it
goal: Your kid designs and plants a real garden: a backyard plot, a raised bed or a few pots on a balcony. They measure the space, work out how many plants really fit, budget the seeds, set harvest dates, then plant it and track what grows.
need: A spot to grow: a garden bed, a raised bed, pots or a sunny windowsill
A tape measure, paper and a pencil (graph paper helps)
Seeds or seedlings, soil and water
Optional: a small budget for seeds and supplies, $5 to $15

lesson.text: Spacing decides what fits, not how small the seed is. Divide the bed by the space each plant needs.
lesson.before: Lettuce seeds are tiny. We'll fit 50 in this bed.

model.line: Needs about 8 in. 48 ÷ 8 = 6 across, 24 ÷ 8 = 3 rows. 6 × 3 = 18 plants.
1 tomato on one half, 3 × 3 = 9 lettuces on the other.

lesson.modelNote: That's the maths this guide practises: measure, divide by the spacing, then decide what's worth the space.

howTo.intro: You don't need teaching experience. You're the garden assistant, not the gardener. Let them choose what to grow, start small (a few pots count), and treat anything that doesn't grow as data, not failure.

plan.what: Pick the spot, measure it and choose what to grow (Steps 1 and 2).
Lay it out, budget it and set the dates (Steps 3 and 4).
Plant, track the growth and do the final maths (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: It's the wrong season to plant outside
troubleshoot.a: Grow fast things indoors on a sunny windowsill: herbs, lettuce or radishes in pots. The measuring, spacing and budgeting work the same way.
Make it a science question: too deep, too dry, too cold, too old? Have them check the seed packet and try again with one change.

skills.name: Measuring
skills.text: real spaces with a real tape

steps.title: Pick the spot and measure it
steps.why: Sun, water and space decide everything else.
steps.kid: Your kid looks at 2 or 3 possible spots and checks the sun (most vegetables need 6 hours or more), how far the water is, and how much room there is. They pick the best one, measure the length and width, and work out the area. Using pots? They measure each one.
steps.you: Walk it together and let them choose. If you're not sure about the sun, check the spot in the morning, at noon and in the late afternoon.
ask: How many hours of sun does this spot get?
What could help or hurt a garden here: shade, wind, animals?
steps.tip: Have them note the sun on the spot at three times of day. It's their first piece of real garden data.

levels.explore: Pick a spot, say why, and measure the length and width.
levels.develop: Compare 2 or 3 spots on sun, water and space, then work out the usable area.
levels.extend: Score each spot from 1 to 5 on sun hours, water and space, and draw the winner to scale.

steps.title: Choose what to grow
steps.why: Matching what they want with what will actually work.
steps.kid: Your kid lists 5 to 10 things they'd like to grow, then checks each one on the seed packet or the Garden Cheat Sheet at the end of the guide: sun, spacing, days to harvest and the right season. They narrow it down to the ones that fit their spot and their time.
steps.you: Help them find the information on seed packets, at a garden centre or online. Ask 'does it fit?' and 'is there time before the cold?'
ask: What do you actually like to eat?
If it takes 90 days and it's already late in the season, will it make it?
steps.tip: Put one fast crop in the plan, like radishes. Sprouts in a week keep kids interested while the slow ones grow.

levels.explore: Pick 2 or 3 plants and find out how much space and sun each needs.
levels.develop: Check 5 plants for sun, water, spacing and harvest time, and choose the best fits.
levels.extend: Build a table for 8 plants with a fit score for your spot, plus which plants grow well together.

steps.title: Lay it out with real spacing
steps.why: Division decides how many plants fit.
steps.kid: Your kid divides the length and width of the bed by each plant's spacing to work out how many fit, then draws a layout: tall plants at the back so they don't shade the short ones, and room to reach in. For pots, it's one big plant or a few small ones per pot.
steps.you: Ask 'did you check the spacing?' and 'can you reach the middle without stepping on anything?' Let them redraw if it doesn't fit.
ask: Your row is 48 inches and lettuce needs 8. How many fit?
Which plants go at the back, and why?
steps.tip: Lay string or sticks on the real bed to mark the rows before drawing. Seeing the spacing on the ground makes the numbers make sense.

levels.explore: Draw a simple map with a label for each plant.
levels.develop: Work out how many of each plant fits and draw the layout using real measurements.
levels.extend: Draw it to scale on graph paper and find what percentage of the bed each crop uses.

steps.title: Budget it and set the dates
steps.why: What it costs, and when you'll eat it.
steps.kid: Your kid lists what they need (seeds, soil, pots, labels), marks what you already have, prices the rest and checks it against the budget. Then they add each plant's days to harvest to the planting date to find its harvest date, and put it all on a calendar. Building a raised bed? They also work out the wood to cut and how much soil fills it: length × width × depth.
steps.you: Set a real budget, like $5 to $15. Ask 'can you grow it from seed instead of buying plants?' and 'what could you use instead of a new pot?'
ask: A bed 4 ft × 2 ft × 1 ft deep: how many cubic feet of soil?
Plant carrots today, 70 days to harvest: what's the date?
steps.tip: Yogurt tubs with holes poked in the bottom make good free pots.

levels.explore: List what to buy, estimate the total, and write when each plant should sprout.
levels.develop: Price everything, make 2 trade-offs to stay on budget, and build a planting calendar.
levels.extend: Work out cost per plant, and plan a second planting a few weeks later for a longer harvest.

steps.title: Plant it, track it, do the final maths
steps.why: The plan becomes real, and the data starts coming in.
steps.kid: Your kid plants following their layout, at the depth on the packet, then waters and labels everything. Every few days they record what sprouted and how tall each plant is. At the end they work out the growth per day and the cost per plant, and whether growing it beat buying it.
steps.you: Let them do the planting and the measuring. Remind them to check in, and ask 'what changed since last time?'
ask: It grew 6 cm in 3 days. How much is that per day?
$12 for 20 plants: what did each one cost?
steps.tip: A ruler pushed into the soil next to one plant makes measuring easy, and gives a great photo every week.

levels.explore: Plant everything, label it, and check it 3 times in the first week.
levels.develop: Keep a growth log for 2 weeks and work out the cost per plant.
levels.extend: Graph the growth, compare sprout days with the packet, and work out how many harvests until the garden pays for itself.

reference.title: Garden Cheat Sheet
reference.intro: Ballpark spacing and timing. Seed packets differ by variety, so always check yours.

items.name: Close together
items.ask: Check it: which of these could you harvest in 2 months?

items.name: Need room

lines.v: about 18 in, 60 to 90 days from a seedling
about 24 in, 60 to 80 days from a seedling

items.ask: Check it: is one big plant worth the space of many small ones?

items.name: Sun

lines.v: under 3 hours, so try another spot

items.ask: Check it: does your spot match what your plants need?

items.name: Grow on a budget

lines.v: a few dollars, often dozens of seeds or more
yogurt tubs and cans with drainage holes
split a packet with a friend or a neighbour
beans and peas are the easiest

items.ask: Check it: what can you reuse instead of buying?

after.label: The garden maths
lines: Plants in a row = row length ÷ spacing
Soil to fill a bed = length × width × depth
Harvest date = planting date + days to harvest
Cost per plant = total spent ÷ number of plants

conclusion.headline: They grew a plan into a garden.
conclusion.text: Your kid measured a real space, worked out how many plants fit, budgeted the seeds, set harvest dates, planted it and tracked the growth. Area, division, money and science, growing right outside the door.
conclusion.celebrate: Ask them to give the family a garden tour: what's planted where, why, and when it'll be ready.
extensions: Weigh every harvest and work out what it would cost at the store
Plan next season's garden with what you learned
Try the same plant in a pot and in the ground, and compare
Build your own raised bed: measure, cut the wood and estimate the soil

signs: They read the back of a seed packet without being asked
They count the days to a harvest on the calendar
They notice which spots in the yard get the most sun
makeItReal: Give your kid one real growing space that's theirs to plan, even if it's a single pot. Let them buy the seeds with the budget and make every decision. A garden they designed is a garden they'll check every morning.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

fromHome.text: In the spring, the kids built our garden. They chose the spot (flat, with lots of sun), measured it, worked out the wood, cut it with their dad, built the bed and estimated how much soil it would take. Then they grew radishes, carrots, beets, cucumbers and tomatoes.
